title: Why God became human
hookLine: Athanasius: he became human that we might become godlike; Anselm asked why a God-man was needed

lines: A STUDENT WHO WON'T LET GO.
cards: A student sits with his teacher, and the student will not let a question go. Why? If God is all-powerful, why not simply forgive?

Why come down at all, be laid in a manger, and die? The teacher is Anselm, an archbishop, and he writes the whole conversation down as a dialogue, titled with the student's question in Latin: Cur Deus Homo.
Why God became human. Long before him, a bishop named Athanasius had given his own answer, in one sentence people still quote. Two answers, one question.

teach.b: Day three hundred met the event itself, in John's Gospel: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Not a visit in disguise. Flesh: hunger, tiredness, tears.

teach.h: ATHANASIUS: SO WE MIGHT BE MADE GOD.
teach.b: Athanasius asked what that was for, and his answer, in an old English translation of his book On the Incarnation, is this: "He was made man that we might be made God." That sounds startling.
He didn't mean people stop being creatures.
He meant what the second letter of Peter means by "partakers of the divine nature": God came all the way into human life so that human life could be drawn all the way into God's.
A doctor doesn't heal from across the street; he comes to the bed. Anselm came at the question from another side. Sin, he argued, is a debt of honor owed to God, and it's humanity that owes it.

teach.h: ANSELM: A DEBT ONLY A GOD-MAN CAN PAY.
teach.b: But the debt is too great for any human to pay; only God could pay it. So the one who pays must be both: human, because humans owe it, and God, because only God can. Hence a God-man.

Christians have carried both answers. Orthodox teachers dwell on Athanasius: God became human to heal and raise humanity into his life. Anselm's argument shaped later Western thinking about the cross.
Other answers sit alongside these, and some are coming soon.
Earlier still, Irenaeus put it in a line today's carry borrows: he became what we are, so that we might become what he is.

how: Christians celebrate the Word made flesh at Christmas and in the creeds, which say that he came down from heaven for us and for our salvation and was made man; Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant teachers explain the why in different, overlapping ways.

games.q: you're Anselm's student. the debt of sin is humanity's to pay, but it's too great for any human. who can pay it?
o: an angel, who is neither God nor human.
one who is both God and human.
games.why: Anselm argued the one who pays must be human, because humans owe it, and God, because only God can. hence a God-man.

practice: Ask the question slowly, the way Anselm's student did, why would God become human, without hurrying to an answer.
Then bring it close to your own body, your hands, your tired back, the hunger that will come around lunchtime, all of which, in Christian teaching, God took on.
If you pray, hold the line from John, the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us; if you don't, just keep the question company.

wordCard.voice: Why God became human. Athanasius: so that we might be made God. Anselm: because only a God-man could pay what humanity owed.

orig.note: Greek: flesh. John 1:14: the Word was made flesh, the word behind the incarnation.

carryVoice: Your line: he became what we are. Hunger and tiredness included. Rest well.
